Key Research Thinking Patterns: Pattern 1: Investigating White Matter Injury with Magnetization Transfer Ratio (MTR) - This study aimed to investigate whether MTR can evaluate the severity of white matter injury in DCM, and the results showed that tract-specific MTR can reflect white matter changes in moderate/severe myelopathy patients (MTR measurements in the ventral reticulospinal tract correlated with upper and lower limb motor mJOA scores).

Pattern 2: Enhancing Perovskite Solar Cells with Non-Fullerene Acceptors - This study introduced Y6-BO and Y7-BO non-fullerene acceptors as interfacial modifiers to enhance the efficiency and stability of inverted perovskite solar cells and modules, achieving record PCE of 25.82% and outstanding efficiencies of 23.06%, 22.32%, and 21.10% for different areas.

Pattern 3: Investigating Functional Connectivity in the Brain - This study investigated the functional connectivity of the default mode network (DMN) in non-hospitalized patients with post-COVID cognitive complaints, finding that DMN connectivity was positively correlated with cognitive performance and associated with clinically significant levels of cognitive impairment.

Pattern 4: Identifying Recurring and Transient Co-Activation Patterns in EEG - This study identified a set of reproducible recurring and transient co-activation patterns (CAPs) in EEG that resemble canonical time-averaged Resting-State Networks (RSNs), suggesting that CAPs can reveal the fast dynamics of brain-wide networked neuronal activations.
Summary Description: Lei Ding is a researcher with expertise in neurology, neurosurgery, biomedical engineering, and materials science. Their work focuses on investigating white matter injury in degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) using magnetization transfer ratio (MTR), developing perovskite solar cells with non-fullerene acceptors to enhance efficiency and stability, and exploring functional connectivity in the brain using EEG and fMRI. They also investigate the feasibility of using median nerve stimulation as a task-based paradigm for assessing spinal cord function in DCM patients. Their research has significant implications for the development of novel diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for neurological disorders and the advancement of renewable energy technologies.
